analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the tax deduction for advertising and promoting prescription drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in the Ways and Means Committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the tax code so drug companies could no longer write off the cost of advertising and promoting prescription drugs — including TV ads aimed at consumers and promotion aimed at doctors, such as free samples, trials, and starter kits. Those costs currently reduce the taxes drug companies pay; the bill would end that. It was referred to the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would collect more federal revenue now that drug marketing costs are no longer a deductible business expense. Patients and doctors could also benefit indirectly: drug companies promote expensive brand-name drugs heavily because marketing has been partially paid for by taxpayers, and removing that write-off raises the after-tax cost of pushing prescriptions up.

how_it_helps.text: Would deny any federal income tax deduction for expenses of advertising or promoting prescription drugs [S2] [S3].

The ban covers direct-to-consumer advertising in any media and promotion directed at doctors and others who decide what drugs to use, including free product samples, free trials, and starter kits [S3].
It would apply to amounts paid or incurred after enactment, in tax years ending after enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical companies, whose marketing budgets would no longer be partially underwritten by federal tax deductions, and the media and advertising businesses that earn revenue from drug ads, which could lose sales.

drawbacks.text: Denying the deduction does not ban drug advertising; it only raises its after-tax cost by roughly the corporate tax rate, so the effect on actual prescribing and prices is uncertain [S3].

The ban covers free samples and starter kits given to doctors; supporters of samples argue they help uninsured and low-income patients get started on medication, so the bill could cut off some of that supply [S3].
Broadcast networks and advertising businesses would lose substantial ad revenue, a real economic cost the bill would shift to them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a modest, well-targeted tax change: marketing expenses would be treated like any other nondeductible expense rather than subsidized by all taxpayers. The costs are real but limited — lost ad revenue for media companies and possible loss of some free samples — and the bill's overall effect on drug prices would depend on how companies respond. It was a narrow, serious proposal that got essentially no support.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marion Berry introduced the bill on November 2, 2009 [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
No action beyond the referral is recorded; the bill received no hearing, markup, or floor vote in the 111th Congress [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical companies keep the federal tax write-off for their advertising and promotion budgets, and the media companies that sell drug ads keep the revenue. Patients and taxpayers are no better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and their ad sellers

for.name: Marion Berry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the tax committee, then took no recorded follow-up.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the tax code
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member besides the sponsor signed on, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never tested.

industries.note: Drug companies currently deduct their advertising and promotion costs — including samples and starter kits aimed at doctors — from their taxable income, meaning taxpayers help pay for the campaigns that steer prescribing toward expensive brand-name drugs. The bill would end that subsidy, so pharma's interest runs against ending it.

Drug companies are heavy buyers of television and other advertising; the bill would deny the deduction that partially offsets those ad buys, and media outlets that depend on that revenue would lose it.
